processing: Solomon's seal root is cut and usually roasted, then simmered or bagged for steeping.
harvest_season: Sold as a dried, roasted root all year; little is documented about harvest timing.
appearance_dry: Pale to golden-brown roasted root pieces, or a fine cut in tea bags.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear light amber, as with other roasted Korean grain and root teas.
taste_profile: Savoury and mildly nutty with a gentle sweetness and a roasted aroma often compared to scorched rice.

brewing.notes: For a pot, sellers suggest 20 to 30 g of root to 2 litres of water, simmered. Bags and extracts vary, so follow the packet and dilute to taste. Hot or cold both work.

vintage_note: No vintages or seasons on the label. It is sold year round as loose roasted root, bags or concentrated extract, and it is best judged by the packing date, as with other roasted herbal teas.
description:
Dunggulle-cha is a Korean infusion of Solomon's seal root, usually roasted. There is no tea plant in it, so as with other root infusions it has no caffeine.

Roasting does most of the work, turning a mild root into something savoury and warm, and in that way it sits close to other Korean roasted drinks.

The cup is gentle: nutty, faintly sweet, with an aroma people compare to scorched rice. Some find it an acquired taste. It is hard to ruin, and it holds up well chilled.

Read the ingredients when buying. Many products called Solomon's seal tea are blends; some are mostly roasted rice, with only a small share of the root.

If you want the pure flavour, choose loose root and simmer a small handful in a large pot of water.
history: Little is documented in detail about the history of dunggulle-cha as a drink. Today it is a widely sold Korean packaged tea, available from several large food brands as bags and extracts.
